summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of Carlita B.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held the improvement periods and family case plans afforded the mother were more than adequate, and directed that abuse and neglect cases be given the highest priority with systems developed to monitor their progress and prevent delay.
key_cases.relevance: Once a petition opens a dependency case, Carlita B. makes prompt movement of that case a judicial obligation rather than an aspiration.
key_cases.quote: Unjustified procedural delays wreak havoc on a child's development, stability and security.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing a one-page order dismissing an abuse and neglect petition, the Court held that a circuit court that sees reasonable cause to believe additional abuse or neglect exists may compel DHHR to investigate and amend the petition, and must enter findings of fact and conclusions of law on the allegations.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the court's power over the content and scope of the agency's petition.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court has the inherent authority to compel the Department to amend its petition to encompass the evidence or allegations

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating the adjudicatory and dispositional orders, the Court held that a Rule 26(a) stipulated adjudication must contain agreed facts supporting court involvement and a statement of the respondent's problems, and that without a proper adjudication the circuit court had no jurisdiction to proceed to disposition.
key_cases.relevance: Opening the case is not enough; the adjudication stage must be completed correctly for the court to retain power.
key_cases.quote: Without properly made findings of abuse and/or neglect at adjudication, a case cannot proceed to disposition

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Diva P. v. Kaufman
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Denying the requested extraordinary relief, the Court held that the prosecuting attorney's statutory role in abuse and neglect matters is to cooperate with DHHR's civil action, and directed that the case plan prepared for the improvement period be submitted to the circuit court.
key_cases.relevance: It governs the roles of prosecutor and Department in filing and maintaining the dependency petition, and requires the case plan to be filed with the court.
key_cases.quote: The legislature has specifically indicated through W.Va.Code § 49-6-10 that prosecutors must cooperate with DHHR's efforts to pursue civil abuse and neglect actions

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held that the Department bears a burden that never shifts to the parent — to prove by clear and convincing evidence the conditions of neglect existing when the petition was filed — and that a bare recital of statutory language does not satisfy the findings requirement, although that error was waived here.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the court deciding the case must enter real findings of fact and conclusions of law rather than reciting the statutory disposition language, though an unpreserved objection to that failure is waived.
key_cases.quote: The proper question is whether the evidence which the State Department of Welfare did present was clear and convincing proof of neglect existing at the time the petition was filed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating the termination order and remanding, the Court held that a circuit court may not terminate parental rights without first adjudicating the parent as having abused or neglected the child, where the same court had expressly concluded three months earlier that the father had not abused or neglected them.
key_cases.relevance: Filing and litigating a petition does not by itself empower the court to act on the child's placement; it is the adjudicatory finding, not the petition, that supplies the authority to dispose of the case.
key_cases.quote: a circuit court may not terminate a parent's rights to his child without first finding that the parent abused or neglected his child
